sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Where lines meet, and concurrency

board_events.text: Where Lines Meet
Two non-parallel roads cross at exactly one junction.
Finding it is just solving the two line equations together.

board_events.caption: Three lines all passing through one point are concurrent.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="360" y2="180" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="180" x2="360" y2="60" stroke="#1a56db" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="210" y1="30" x2="210" y2="210" stroke="#c026d3" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="210" cy="120" r="5" fill="#333"/><text x="218" y="116" font-size="11" fill="#333">concurrent point</text></svg>

board_events.text: Three lines through one point are concurrent — a very common exam setup.
You could intersect two and test the third, but a determinant does it in one shot.
A unique intersection needs non-parallel lines: $a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 \ne 0$.
Parallel lines never meet; coincident lines meet everywhere.

segments.text: Let's talk about where lines meet — one of the most heavily tested ideas in the whole chapter.
Two roads that are not parallel cross at exactly one junction. There is one meeting point, no more.
Finding that junction algebraically is nothing fancy: it is just solving the two line equations together, the pair of x and y that satisfies both.
Now scale up. When do three roads all meet at a single roundabout? Look at the picture — three lines threading one common point.
That situation is called concurrency, and it appears again and again, in medians meeting, altitudes meeting, and so on.
You could find where two of them cross and then check the third passes through it — but there is a slicker determinant test that settles it in a single computation.
One caution: a unique intersection only exists when the lines are not parallel, which the algebra encodes as a one b two minus a two b one, not equal to zero.
If that quantity is zero, the lines are either parallel and never meet, or coincident and meet everywhere.
बात करते हैं कि lines कहाँ मिलती हैं — पूरे chapter का सबसे ज़्यादा test होने वाला idea।
दो roads जो parallel नहीं हैं, ठीक एक junction पर cross करती हैं। एक ही meeting point, बस।
उस junction को algebraically ढूँढना कोई fancy चीज़ नहीं: बस दोनों line equations को साथ solve करना, वो x और y जो दोनों को satisfy करे।
अब scale up करो। तीन roads एक ही roundabout पर कब मिलती हैं? picture देखो — तीन lines एक common point से गुज़रती हुई।
इसे concurrency कहते हैं, और यह बार-बार आता है, medians के मिलने में, altitudes के मिलने में, वग़ैरह।
तुम दो का crossing ढूँढकर तीसरी को check कर सकते हो — पर एक slicker determinant test है जो इसे एक ही computation में तय कर देता है।
एक caution: unique intersection तभी होता है जब lines parallel न हों, जिसे algebra a one b two minus a two b one, zero के बराबर नहीं, से लिखता है।
अगर वो quantity zero हो, तो lines या तो parallel हैं और कभी नहीं मिलतीं, या coincident हैं और हर जगह मिलती हैं।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: The family trick

board_events.text: The Family Trick: $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$
Suppose $L_1 = 0$ and $L_2 = 0$ cross at a junction $J$.

board_events.caption: Every line L1 + lambda L2 = 0 passes through the junction J.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="60" y1="60" x2="360" y2="200" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="200" x2="360" y2="60" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="60" x2="320" y2="200" stroke="#c026d3" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="110" y1="200" x2="310" y2="60" stroke="#c026d3" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="210" y1="30" x2="210" y2="230" stroke="#c026d3" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="210" cy="130" r="4.5" fill="#333"/><text x="216" y="126" font-size="12" fill="#333">J</text><text x="70" y="66" font-size="11" fill="#059669">L1 = 0</text><text x="70" y="200" font-size="11" fill="#059669">L2 = 0</text><text x="300" y="248" font-size="10" fill="#c026d3">family through J</text></svg>

board_events.text: At $J$, both $L_1$ and $L_2$ are zero, so the combination is automatically zero too.
So this is a whole family of lines through $J$ — one line for each value of $\lambda$.
The family captures every line through $J$ except $L_2 = 0$ itself (that needs $\lambda \to \infty$).
Impose one extra condition to pin down $\lambda$ — you never compute $J$ at all.

segments.text: <curious>Here is the cleverest single idea in the whole chapter — and it feels like magic the first time.</curious>
Suppose two lines, L one equals zero and L two equals zero, cross at some junction J.
Now watch the picture: every one of these dashed lines passes through J too. What are they?
Consider the combination L one plus lambda times L two. At the junction J, both L one and L two are exactly zero, so the whole combination is automatically zero there, whatever lambda is.
In symbols, L one plus lambda L two equals zero.
So this single expression is a whole family of lines, all passing through J, one line for each value of lambda you choose.
One fine print: this family reaches every line through J except L two itself, which would need lambda running off to infinity. If your answer might be L two, check it on its own.
And the payoff: if you need the line through J that also meets one more condition, just impose that condition to fix lambda — you never have to find J at all.
<curious>यह रहा पूरे chapter का सबसे clever idea — और पहली बार यह जादू जैसा लगता है।</curious>
मान लो दो lines, L one बराबर zero और L two बराबर zero, किसी junction J पर cross करती हैं।
अब picture देखो: इन dashed lines में से हर एक भी J से गुज़रती है। ये क्या हैं?
Combination L one plus lambda times L two सोचो। Junction J पर L one और L two दोनों बिल्कुल zero हैं, तो पूरी combination वहाँ अपने-आप zero हो जाती है, lambda चाहे कुछ भी हो।
Symbols में, L one plus lambda L two बराबर zero।
तो यह अकेली expression lines का एक पूरा family है, सब J से गुज़रती हुई, हर चुने lambda के लिए एक line।
एक fine print: यह family J से गुज़रती हर line तक पहुँचता है सिवाय L two के, जिसके लिए lambda infinity तक जाना पड़ेगा। अगर तुम्हारा answer L two हो सकता है, उसे अलग से check करो।
और payoff: अगर तुम्हें J से गुज़रती वो line चाहिए जो एक और condition भी पूरी करे, तो बस वो condition impose करके lambda fix कर लो — J ढूँढने की ज़रूरत ही नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Proof: the family passes through the junction

board_events.text: Proof: The Family Passes Through $J$
Let $L_1 \equiv a_1 x + b_1 y + c_1$ and $L_2 \equiv a_2 x + b_2 y + c_2$ meet at $J(x_0, y_0)$.
Since $J$ lies on both lines, each expression vanishes there.
So $J$ satisfies $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$ for every $\lambda$.
And $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$ is first-degree, so it is itself a line through $J$.
'Both zero $\Rightarrow$ sum zero' — that is the whole reason the trick works.

segments.text: Let's prove that the family really does pass through the junction — it is a two-line argument.
Write L one as a one x plus b one y plus c one, and L two as a two x plus b two y plus c two, meeting at the junction J with coordinates x nought, y nought.
Because J sits on both lines, each of these expressions evaluates to zero when you plug in J.
That is, L one at J is zero, and L two at J is zero.
Now form the combination at J: L one at J plus lambda times L two at J is zero plus lambda times zero, which is zero.
So J satisfies L one plus lambda L two equals zero for every single value of lambda — the junction is on all of them.
And since L one plus lambda L two is still a first-degree expression, its graph is a line, so it is genuinely a line through J.
The entire trick rests on that one clean fact: both zero implies the sum is zero. That is why the junction rides along for free.
चलो prove करें कि family सचमुच junction से गुज़रता है — यह दो-line वाला argument है।
L one को a one x plus b one y plus c one लिखो, और L two को a two x plus b two y plus c two, जो junction J पर मिलती हैं, coordinates x nought, y nought के साथ।
क्योंकि J दोनों lines पर है, J डालने पर इनमें से हर expression zero हो जाता है।
यानी L one at J zero है, और L two at J zero है।
अब J पर combination बनाओ: L one at J plus lambda times L two at J है zero plus lambda times zero, जो zero है।
तो J, L one plus lambda L two बराबर zero को हर एक lambda के लिए satisfy करता है — junction सब पर है।
और चूँकि L one plus lambda L two अभी भी first-degree expression है, इसका graph एक line है, तो यह सचमुच J से गुज़रती line है।
पूरा trick उसी एक clean fact पर टिका है: both zero मतलब sum zero। इसीलिए junction मुफ़्त में साथ चलता है।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Proof: the concurrency determinant, and the family procedure

board_events.text: Proof: The Concurrency Determinant
Three lines $L_i \equiv a_i x + b_i y + c_i = 0$, with no two parallel.
Let $L_1, L_2$ meet at $J(x_0, y_0)$; concurrency means $L_3$ also passes through $J$.

board_events.latex: \begin{pmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_0 \\ y_0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{0}

board_events.text: This homogeneous system has the nonzero solution $(x_0, y_0, 1)$.
A homogeneous system has a nonzero solution only if its determinant vanishes.

board_events.latex: \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0

board_events.text: Family procedure: write $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$, impose the extra condition, then solve for $\lambda$.
Through a point $\Rightarrow$ substitute it; given slope $\Rightarrow$ set $-A/B$; perpendicular $\Rightarrow$ slope product $-1$.

segments.text: Now the determinant test for concurrency, and why it works.
Take three lines, L one, L two, L three, in general form, and assume no two of them are parallel.
Let the first two meet at the junction J. Concurrency simply means the third line also passes through that same J.
So all three equations hold at J. Stack them as a matrix of coefficients times the column x nought, y nought, one, and the result is the zero vector.
That is a homogeneous system, and it has a genuinely nonzero solution, namely x nought, y nought, one — the last entry is one, so it cannot be all zeros.
Here is the key algebra fact: a homogeneous system can have a nonzero solution only if its coefficient determinant is zero.
So concurrency forces that three by three determinant of the coefficients to vanish. That is the whole test.
And the family procedure in practice: write L one plus lambda L two equals zero, impose whatever extra condition the problem gives, and solve for lambda.
If it must pass through a point, substitute the point; if it has a given slope, set minus A over B equal to it; if it is perpendicular to something, set the slope product to minus one.
अब concurrency के लिए determinant test, और यह क्यों काम करता है।
तीन lines लो, L one, L two, L three, general form में, और मान लो इनमें से कोई दो parallel नहीं।
पहली दो को junction J पर मिलने दो। Concurrency का बस इतना मतलब है कि तीसरी line भी उसी J से गुज़रती है।
तो तीनों equations J पर hold करती हैं। Coefficients के matrix को column x nought, y nought, one से multiply करो, और result zero vector है।
यह एक homogeneous system है, और इसका एक सचमुच nonzero solution है, यानी x nought, y nought, one — आख़िरी entry one है, तो यह पूरा zero नहीं हो सकता।
यह रहा key algebra fact: homogeneous system का nonzero solution तभी हो सकता है जब उसका coefficient determinant zero हो।
तो concurrency उस three by three coefficient determinant को zero होने पर मजबूर कर देती है। यही पूरा test है।
और practice में family procedure: L one plus lambda L two बराबर zero लिखो, problem जो भी extra condition दे उसे impose करो, और lambda के लिए solve करो।
अगर किसी point से गुज़रनी हो, point substitute करो; given slope हो, minus A over B उसके बराबर रखो; किसी चीज़ के perpendicular हो, slope product minus one रखो।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Intersection and family: formula toolkit

board_events.text: Intersection & Family — Toolkit

board_events.latex: \text{Cramer: } x = \frac{b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}, \quad y = \frac{c_1 a_2 - c_2 a_1}{a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1}
\text{Concurrency: } \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 0

board_events.text: The concurrency test assumes no two of the three lines are parallel.

segments.text: Here is the toolkit for intersection, parallelism, concurrency, and the family trick.
The intersection point by Cramer's rule: x is b one c two minus b two c one, over a one b two minus a two b one; y has the same denominator with c one a two minus c two a one on top.
Two lines are parallel and distinct when the a-ratio equals the b-ratio but differs from the c-ratio.
They intersect when the a-ratio is not equal to the b-ratio.
And they are coincident when all three ratios are equal — the same line written twice.
Three lines are concurrent when the three by three determinant of their coefficients is zero.
And the family through a junction is L one plus lambda L two equals zero.
One standing caveat: the concurrency test assumes no two of the three lines are parallel, so always sanity-check that.
यह रहा intersection, parallelism, concurrency, और family trick का toolkit।
Cramer's rule से intersection point: x है b one c two minus b two c one, over a one b two minus a two b one; y का denominator वही, ऊपर c one a two minus c two a one।
दो lines parallel और distinct हैं जब a-ratio बराबर b-ratio हो पर c-ratio से अलग हो।
वे intersect करती हैं जब a-ratio, b-ratio के बराबर न हो।
और coincident हैं जब तीनों ratios बराबर हों — वही line दो बार लिखी हुई।
तीन lines concurrent हैं जब उनके coefficients का three by three determinant zero हो।
और junction से family है L one plus lambda L two बराबर zero।
एक standing caveat: concurrency test मानता है कि तीनों में कोई दो parallel नहीं, तो हमेशा यह sanity-check करो।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Worked examples: intersection and concurrency

board_events.text: Worked: Intersection & Concurrency
Example 1: intersection of $2x + 3y - 8 = 0$ and $x - y + 1 = 0$.
Example 2: are $x+y-2=0$, $2x-y-1=0$, $4x-y-5=0$ concurrent?
Determinant is $6 \ne 0$, so the lines are NOT concurrent.
Anchor the $+\,-\,+$ signs across the top row and expand slowly.

segments.text: Two examples: a plain intersection, then a concurrency check by determinant.
Example one: find where two x plus three y minus eight equals zero meets x minus y plus one equals zero.
From the second line, x equals y minus one. Substitute into the first: two times y minus one, plus three y minus eight, equals zero, which gives five y equals ten.
So y is two and x is one; the intersection is the point one comma two.
Example two: are the three lines x plus y minus two, two x minus y minus one, and four x minus y minus five all concurrent?
Drop straight into the determinant — do not solve two and test the third. Expanding along the top row gives four, minus a negative six, minus four, which is six.
The determinant is six, which is not zero, so the three lines are not concurrent.
The only trap here is a sign slip in the cofactor expansion, so anchor the plus, minus, plus pattern across the top row and expand slowly.
दो examples: एक plain intersection, फिर determinant से concurrency check।
Example one: ढूँढो कि two x plus three y minus eight बराबर zero, x minus y plus one बराबर zero से कहाँ मिलती है।
दूसरी line से, x बराबर y minus one। पहली में substitute करो: two times y minus one, plus three y minus eight, बराबर zero, जो देता है five y बराबर ten।
तो y है two और x है one; intersection है point one comma two।
Example two: क्या तीन lines x plus y minus two, two x minus y minus one, और four x minus y minus five सब concurrent हैं?
सीधे determinant में उतरो — दो solve करके तीसरी test मत करो। Top row के साथ expand करने पर मिलता है four, minus a negative six, minus four, जो है six।
Determinant है six, जो zero नहीं, तो तीनों lines concurrent नहीं हैं।
यहाँ एकमात्र trap है cofactor expansion में sign slip, तो top row के साथ plus, minus, plus pattern anchor करो और धीरे expand करो।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Worked example: the family method

board_events.text: Worked: The Family Method
Find the line through the intersection of $x+2y-5=0$ and $3x-y+1=0$ that also passes through $(2,1)$.
Impose passage through the point $(2,1)$:
We never computed the intersection point — that is the payoff.

segments.text: <excited>Now the family method in action — watch us solve without ever finding the intersection.</excited>
Find the line through the intersection of x plus two y minus five and three x minus y plus one that also passes through the point two comma one.
Write the family: the quantity x plus two y minus five, plus lambda times the quantity three x minus y plus one, equals zero.
Now impose the extra condition that it passes through two comma one — just substitute those coordinates.
That gives two plus two minus five, plus lambda times six minus one plus one, equals zero, which is minus one plus six lambda equals zero.
So lambda is one sixth.
Substitute lambda back, clear the fraction, and you get nine x plus eleven y minus twenty nine equals zero.
And notice the whole point: we never computed the intersection of the two lines. Skipping that step is exactly the elegance examiners reward.
<excited>अब family method action में — देखो हम intersection ढूँढे बिना ही solve करते हैं।</excited>
x plus two y minus five और three x minus y plus one के intersection से गुज़रती वो line ढूँढो जो point two comma one से भी गुज़रे।
Family लिखो: the quantity x plus two y minus five, plus lambda times the quantity three x minus y plus one, बराबर zero।
अब extra condition impose करो कि यह two comma one से गुज़रती है — बस वो coordinates substitute करो।
इससे मिलता है two plus two minus five, plus lambda times six minus one plus one, बराबर zero, यानी minus one plus six lambda बराबर zero।
तो lambda है one sixth।
Lambda वापस substitute करो, fraction clear करो, और मिलता है nine x plus eleven y minus twenty nine बराबर zero।
और पूरी बात यही: हमने दोनों lines का intersection कभी compute नहीं किया। उस step को skip करना ही वो elegance है जो examiners reward करते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Worked example: concurrency with a parameter (advanced)

board_events.text: Worked: Concurrency with a Parameter (Advanced)
For what $a$ are $ax+2y+1=0$, $2x+ay+2=0$, $x+y-1=0$ concurrent?
At $a=2$ the first two lines become parallel — concurrency is impossible; discard it.

segments.text: <curious>An Advanced twist: solving the determinant is only half the job — the parallel-check is the trap.</curious>
For what value of a are the lines a x plus two y plus one, two x plus a y plus two, and x plus y minus one all concurrent?
Set the coefficient determinant to zero.
Expanding along the top row: a times minus a minus two, minus two times minus two minus two, plus the quantity two minus a. That collapses to minus a squared minus three a plus ten equals zero.
Multiply through by minus one: a squared plus three a minus ten equals zero, which factors as a plus five, times a minus two.
So a is minus five or a is two — two candidates from the algebra.

Now the Advanced check. At a equals two, the first two lines become two x plus two y plus one and two x plus two y plus two — parallel and distinct, so they never meet, and concurrency is impossible. Discard a equals two.
At a equals minus five, no two lines are parallel, so it survives. The single valid answer is a equals minus five.
<curious>एक Advanced twist: determinant solve करना आधा काम है — parallel-check ही trap है।</curious>
किस a के लिए lines a x plus two y plus one, two x plus a y plus two, और x plus y minus one सब concurrent हैं?
Coefficient determinant को zero रखो।
Top row से expand: a times minus a minus two, minus two times minus two minus two, plus the quantity two minus a। यह गिरकर बनता है minus a squared minus three a plus ten बराबर zero।
Minus one से multiply करो: a squared plus three a minus ten बराबर zero, जो factor होता है a plus five, times a minus two।
तो a है minus five या a है two — algebra से दो candidates।

अब Advanced check। a बराबर two पर, पहली दो lines बन जाती हैं two x plus two y plus one और two x plus two y plus two — parallel और distinct, तो वे कभी नहीं मिलतीं, और concurrency असंभव है। a बराबर two discard करो।
a बराबर minus five पर कोई दो lines parallel नहीं, तो यह बच जाता है। एकमात्र valid answer है a बराबर minus five।

sections.subtopic: Point of Intersection, Concurrency and Family of Lines
sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: intersection and family

board_events.text: Pitfalls: Intersection & Family
If a line passes through an intersection plus one condition, use $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$ — skip finding the point.
After the concurrency determinant is zero, still check that no two lines are parallel.
The family $L_1 + \lambda L_2 = 0$ misses $L_2$ itself — test that case separately if needed.
Keep the $+\,-\,+$ sign pattern explicit when expanding a determinant.
Pro-tip: 'line through the intersection of ... and ...' should trigger the family trick instantly.
Finding the point first is almost always the slower, more error-prone path.
Determinant dies $\Rightarrow$ they meet — with the no-two-parallel caveat.

segments.text: Let's close this subtopic with the traps and the one habit that saves the most time.
Trap one, really a time-saver: if a question wants a line through an intersection plus one more condition, reach for L one plus lambda L two equals zero and skip finding the point entirely.
Trap two: a zero concurrency determinant can also be satisfied by a degenerate, parallel configuration, so always verify that no two of the lines are parallel.
Trap three: the family L one plus lambda L two can produce every line through the junction except L two itself. If L two might be your answer, test that case on its own.
Trap four: when expanding a three by three determinant, keep the plus, minus, plus sign pattern explicit across your chosen row — rushing the middle term is where marks vanish.
<whisper>And the pro-tip: the phrase 'line through the intersection of, and' should trigger the family trick instantly, before you write anything else.</whisper>
Finding the intersection point first is almost always the slower path, and it introduces extra arithmetic to slip on.
Sum it up as: determinant dies, they meet — always with the no-two-parallel caveat attached.
इस subtopic को traps और उस एक आदत के साथ बंद करते हैं जो सबसे ज़्यादा time बचाती है।
Trap one, असल में time-saver: अगर सवाल intersection से गुज़रती line plus एक और condition माँगे, तो L one plus lambda L two बराबर zero लो और point ढूँढना पूरी तरह skip करो।
Trap two: zero concurrency determinant एक degenerate, parallel configuration से भी satisfy हो सकता है, तो हमेशा verify करो कि कोई दो lines parallel नहीं।
Trap three: family L one plus lambda L two junction से गुज़रती हर line बना सकता है सिवाय L two के। अगर L two तुम्हारा answer हो सकता है, उसे अलग से test करो।
Trap four: three by three determinant expand करते समय अपनी chosen row पर plus, minus, plus sign pattern explicit रखो — बीच का term जल्दबाज़ी में करना ही marks खाता है।
<whisper>और pro-tip: phrase 'line through the intersection of, and' को family trick तुरंत trigger करना चाहिए, कुछ और लिखने से पहले।</whisper>
पहले intersection point ढूँढना लगभग हमेशा slower रास्ता है, और इसमें slip करने को extra arithmetic आ जाता है।
इसे ऐसे याद रखो: determinant dies, they meet — हमेशा no-two-parallel caveat के साथ।

board_events.text: Angle Bisectors: the Equidistant Lines
When two lines cross they make four angles; the bisectors split them exactly in half.

board_events.caption: The two angle bisectors are always perpendicular to each other.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="60" y1="190" x2="360" y2="70" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="70" x2="360" y2="190" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="130" x2="360" y2="130" stroke="#1a56db" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><line x1="210" y1="20" x2="210" y2="240" stroke="#1a56db" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/><circle cx="210" cy="130" r="3.5" fill="#333"/><text x="216" y="126" font-size="11" fill="#333">O</text><text x="298" y="122" font-size="11" fill="#1a56db">bisector</text><text x="216" y="36" font-size="11" fill="#1a56db">bisector</text><text x="66" y="202" font-size="11" fill="#059669">line 1</text><text x="66" y="66" font-size="11" fill="#059669">line 2</text></svg>

board_events.text: A point lies on a bisector exactly when it is equidistant from the two lines.
Dropping the moduli introduces a $\pm$ — the two signs give the two bisectors.
The identification rules require both constants positive first — normalize $c_1, c_2 > 0$.
The two bisectors are always perpendicular — a free check on every answer.

segments.text: When two lines cross, they make four angles in two equal pairs, and the bisectors are the lines that split those angles exactly in half.
Look at the picture: two crossing lines, and their two bisectors. Notice something — the bisectors sit at right angles to each other, always.
Because they bisect supplementary angles, once you have one bisector, the other is automatically perpendicular to it.
The defining property is beautifully simple: a point lies on a bisector exactly when it is the same perpendicular distance from both lines. Equidistant means on the bisector.
Since distance from a line is that familiar expression over the root of a squared plus b squared, equidistant becomes the first ratio equal to plus or minus the second.
Dropping the two moduli is what introduces the plus or minus, and that single sign choice is the whole story: the two signs give the two bisectors.
One crucial setup: the clean identification rules only work if you first rewrite both lines with positive constant terms. Skip that and every sign rule inverts on you.
And keep in mind the free check: whatever two bisectors you compute, they must come out perpendicular.
जब दो lines cross करती हैं, तो चार angles बनते हैं दो equal pairs में, और bisectors वे lines हैं जो उन angles को ठीक आधा बाँटती हैं।
Picture देखो: दो crossing lines, और उनके दो bisectors। एक बात देखो — bisectors एक दूसरे के right angles पर बैठते हैं, हमेशा।
क्योंकि वे supplementary angles को bisect करते हैं, एक bisector मिलते ही दूसरा अपने-आप उसके perpendicular होता है।
Defining property बेहद simple है: एक point bisector पर तभी होता है जब वो दोनों lines से same perpendicular distance पर हो। Equidistant मतलब bisector पर।
चूँकि line से distance वही familiar expression over root of a squared plus b squared है, equidistant बन जाता है पहला ratio बराबर plus या minus दूसरा।
दोनों moduli हटाना ही plus या minus लाता है, और वही एक sign choice पूरी कहानी है: दो signs दो bisectors देते हैं।
एक crucial setup: clean identification rules तभी काम करते हैं जब तुम पहले दोनों lines को positive constant terms के साथ लिखो। इसे skip करो तो हर sign rule उलट जाता है।
और free check याद रखो: जो भी दो bisectors compute करो, वे perpendicular आने ही चाहिए।

sections.title: Proof: the bisector is the equidistant locus

board_events.text: Proof: The Bisector is the Equidistant Locus
A point $P$ is equidistant from lines $L_1$ and $L_2$.

board_events.caption: Equal perpendicular distances from P to both lines.
board_events.svg: <svg font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" viewBox="0 0 420 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="120" y1="200" x2="320" y2="40" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120" y1="200" x2="390" y2="160" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/><text x="322" y="40" font-size="11" fill="#059669">L1</text><text x="392" y="162" font-size="11" fill="#059669">L2</text><circle cx="120" cy="200" r="3" fill="#333"/><circle cx="270" cy="120" r="4" fill="#c026d3"/><text x="276" y="116" font-size="12" fill="#c026d3">P</text><line x1="270" y1="120" x2="238" y2="94" stroke="#c026d3" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="270" y1="120" x2="286" y2="158" stroke="#c026d3" stroke-width="1.3" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="212" y="90" font-size="10" fill="#666">equal</text><text x="292" y="156" font-size="10" fill="#666">equal</text></svg>

board_events.text: Removing the moduli gives two cases — the expressions equal, or negatives of each other.
Each sign is a first-degree equation, hence a line — together, the two bisectors.
Each line gets its OWN denominator $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ — never share one.

segments.text: Let's prove that the bisector really is the locus of equidistant points — it follows straight from the distance formula.
Take a point P that is equidistant from the two lines L one and L two.
Picture it: the perpendicular from P to the first line and the perpendicular to the second are the same length.
Write that as an equation using the point-to-line distance: the modulus of L one over its own root equals the modulus of L two over its own root.
Now remove the moduli. Two expressions can have equal absolute values in exactly two ways — they are equal, or they are negatives of each other.
That is exactly the plus or minus: the first ratio equals plus or minus the second.
Each choice of sign is a first-degree equation, so each is a line. Together, those two lines are the two angle bisectors.
One thing students routinely botch: each line carries its own denominator, the root of its own a squared plus b squared. Never share a single denominator across both.
चलो prove करें कि bisector सचमुच equidistant points का locus है — यह सीधे distance formula से निकलता है।
एक point P लो जो दोनों lines L one और L two से equidistant है।
Picture करो: P से पहली line तक perpendicular और दूसरी तक perpendicular same length के हैं।
इसे point-to-line distance से equation लिखो: L one का modulus over उसका अपना root बराबर L two का modulus over उसका अपना root।
अब moduli हटाओ। दो expressions के absolute values ठीक दो तरीक़ों से बराबर हो सकते हैं — या तो वे equal हों, या एक दूसरे के negatives हों।
यही तो plus या minus है: पहला ratio बराबर plus या minus दूसरा।
हर sign choice एक first-degree equation है, तो हर एक line है। साथ में, वे दो lines ही दो angle bisectors हैं।
एक चीज़ जो students अक्सर बिगाड़ते हैं: हर line अपना denominator रखती है, अपने a squared plus b squared का root। दोनों पर एक ही denominator कभी share मत करो।

board_events.text: Which Bisector Is Which?
Step 1: rewrite both lines so the constants are positive, $c_1, c_2 > 0$.
Step 2: the $+$ sign gives the bisector of the angle containing the origin.
Why positive constants? They pin the origin to the 'positive' side of both lines.
Step 3: to label acute versus obtuse, compute $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2$ with the positive forms.

board_events.latex: a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 > 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{'+' is the obtuse bisector}
a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 < 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{'+' is the acute bisector}

board_events.text: The two bisectors always satisfy $m_1 m_2 = -1$ — verify at the end.

segments.text: Writing the two bisectors is easy; the real exam skill is telling which is which. Here is the procedure.
Step one: rewrite both lines so their constant terms are positive. If a constant is negative, multiply that whole equation by minus one.
Step two: with both constants positive, the plus sign always gives the bisector of the angle that contains the origin.

Why does forcing positive constants matter? Because the sign of the constant encodes which side of the line the origin is on; making both positive pins the origin to the positive side of both, and that is what makes the plus sign mean the origin's angle.
Step three: to label acute versus obtuse, compute a one a two plus b one b two, using the positive-constant forms.
If that sum is positive, the plus bisector is the obtuse one.
If that sum is negative, the plus bisector is the acute one.
And whatever you get, the two bisectors must satisfy m one times m two equals minus one — verify that perpendicularity at the end as a check.
दो bisectors लिखना आसान है; असली exam skill है यह बताना कि कौन-सा कौन-सा है। यह रही procedure।
Step one: दोनों lines को ऐसे लिखो कि उनके constant terms positive हों। अगर कोई constant negative हो, तो उस पूरी equation को minus one से multiply करो।
Step two: दोनों constants positive होने पर, plus sign हमेशा उस angle का bisector देता है जिसमें origin है।

Positive constants ज़रूरी क्यों? क्योंकि constant का sign बताता है origin line के किस side है; दोनों को positive करना origin को दोनों के positive side पर pin कर देता है, और यही plus sign को origin के angle का मतलब देता है।
Step three: acute बनाम obtuse label करने के लिए, positive-constant forms से a one a two plus b one b two निकालो।
अगर वो sum positive हो, तो plus bisector obtuse वाला है।
अगर वो sum negative हो, तो plus bisector acute वाला है।
और जो भी मिले, दोनों bisectors को m one times m two बराबर minus one satisfy करना चाहिए — अंत में वो perpendicularity check कर लो।

board_events.text: Angle Bisectors — Toolkit
Normalize first: make $c_1 > 0$ and $c_2 > 0$.

board_events.latex: a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 > 0 \Rightarrow \text{'+' obtuse}; \quad < 0 \Rightarrow \text{'+' acute}

board_events.text: Decide acute versus obtuse only when the question asks for it.
Each line carries its own $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ denominator — do not share one.

segments.text: Here is the whole toolkit for angle bisectors on one board.
The pair of bisectors: the first line over its root equals plus or minus the second line over its root.
Before anything else, normalize: make both constant terms positive.
With that done, the plus sign is the bisector of the angle containing the origin.
For acute versus obtuse, look at a one a two plus b one b two: positive means the plus bisector is obtuse, negative means the plus bisector is acute.
But only bother with this when the question actually asks acute or obtuse — do not compute it out of habit.
And always, the slopes of the two bisectors multiply to minus one.
Finally, remember each line keeps its own root of a squared plus b squared in the denominator; do not share one across both.
यह रहा angle bisectors का पूरा toolkit एक board पर।
Bisectors का pair: पहली line over उसका root बराबर plus या minus दूसरी line over उसका root।
सबसे पहले normalize करो: दोनों constant terms positive बनाओ।
यह करने पर, plus sign उस angle का bisector है जिसमें origin है।
Acute बनाम obtuse के लिए, a one a two plus b one b two देखो: positive मतलब plus bisector obtuse, negative मतलब plus bisector acute।
पर इसकी परवाह तभी करो जब सवाल सचमुच acute या obtuse माँगे — आदत से मत compute करो।
और हमेशा, दोनों bisectors की slopes multiply होकर minus one देती हैं।
आख़िर में, याद रखो हर line denominator में अपना root of a squared plus b squared रखती है; दोनों पर एक share मत करो।

sections.title: Worked examples: both bisectors and the origin's bisector

board_events.text: Worked: Both Bisectors & the Origin's
Example 1: bisectors of $3x - 4y + 7 = 0$ and $5x + 12y - 2 = 0$.
Example 2: origin's bisector of $4x + 3y - 6 = 0$ and $5x + 12y + 9 = 0$.
Make constants positive: rewrite the first as $-4x - 3y + 6 = 0$.

segments.text: Two examples: first write both bisectors, then pick out just the origin's bisector.
Example one: the bisectors of three x minus four y plus seven and five x plus twelve y minus two.
The roots are five and thirteen, so set three x minus four y plus seven over five equal to plus or minus five x plus twelve y minus two over thirteen.
Take the plus sign, cross-multiply, and simplify to fourteen x minus one hundred twelve y plus one hundred one equals zero.
Take the minus sign and you get sixty four x plus eight y plus eighty one equals zero. Those are the two bisectors.
Example two: find only the bisector of the angle containing the origin for four x plus three y minus six and five x plus twelve y plus nine.
First make constants positive. The first has a negative six, so multiply it by minus one to get minus four x minus three y plus six. The second already has plus nine.
Now take the plus sign: minus four x minus three y plus six over five equals five x plus twelve y plus nine over thirteen.
Cross-multiply and simplify, and the origin's bisector is seven x plus nine y minus three equals zero.
दो examples: पहले दोनों bisectors लिखो, फिर सिर्फ़ origin वाला bisector चुनो।
Example one: three x minus four y plus seven और five x plus twelve y minus two के bisectors।
Roots हैं five और thirteen, तो three x minus four y plus seven over five को plus या minus five x plus twelve y minus two over thirteen के बराबर रखो।
Plus sign लो, cross-multiply करो, और simplify करके मिलता है fourteen x minus one hundred twelve y plus one hundred one बराबर zero।
Minus sign लो तो मिलता है sixty four x plus eight y plus eighty one बराबर zero। ये दो bisectors हैं।
Example two: four x plus three y minus six और five x plus twelve y plus nine के लिए सिर्फ़ origin वाले angle का bisector ढूँढो।
पहले constants positive करो। पहली में negative six है, तो उसे minus one से multiply करके minus four x minus three y plus six बनाओ। दूसरी में पहले से plus nine है।
अब plus sign लो: minus four x minus three y plus six over five बराबर five x plus twelve y plus nine over thirteen।
Cross-multiply और simplify करो, और origin का bisector है seven x plus nine y minus three बराबर zero।

sections.title: Worked example: identifying the acute bisector

board_events.text: Worked: Identifying the Acute Bisector
For $x + y - 2 = 0$ and $7x - y + 3 = 0$, find the acute-angle bisector.
Make constants positive: rewrite the first as $-x - y + 2 = 0$.
With positive constants and $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 < 0$, the '+' sign is the acute bisector.
Normalize constants first, then read the acute/obtuse rule — order matters.

segments.text: Now the harder skill: not just writing a bisector, but identifying the acute one.
For x plus y minus two and seven x minus y plus three, find the acute-angle bisector.
First make constants positive. The first line has a negative constant, so rewrite it as minus x minus y plus two. The second already has plus three.
Now compute a one a two plus b one b two with these forms: minus one times seven, plus minus one times minus one, which is minus seven plus one, that is minus six.
Since the constants are positive and this sum is negative, the rule tells us the plus sign gives the acute bisector.
So take the plus sign: minus x minus y plus two over root two equals seven x minus y plus three over root fifty.
Since root fifty is five root two, multiply both sides by five root two and simplify, giving twelve x plus four y minus seven equals zero — the acute-angle bisector.
The order is everything here: normalize the constants first, then read the acute-obtuse rule. Reverse them and the rule points the wrong way.
अब कठिन skill: सिर्फ़ bisector लिखना नहीं, बल्कि acute वाला identify करना।
x plus y minus two और seven x minus y plus three के लिए acute-angle bisector ढूँढो।
पहले constants positive करो। पहली line का constant negative है, तो उसे minus x minus y plus two लिखो। दूसरी में पहले से plus three है।
अब इन forms से a one a two plus b one b two निकालो: minus one times seven, plus minus one times minus one, जो है minus seven plus one, यानी minus six।
चूँकि constants positive हैं और यह sum negative है, rule कहता है plus sign acute bisector देता है।
तो plus sign लो: minus x minus y plus two over root two बराबर seven x minus y plus three over root fifty।
चूँकि root fifty है five root two, दोनों sides को five root two से multiply करके simplify करो, तो मिलता है twelve x plus four y minus seven बराबर zero — acute-angle bisector।
यहाँ order ही सब कुछ है: पहले constants normalize करो, फिर acute-obtuse rule पढ़ो। इन्हें उलटो तो rule ग़लत दिशा में इशारा करता है।

board_events.text: Worked: Bisectors Are Perpendicular (Advanced)
Verify perpendicularity for the two bisectors found in Example 1.
Why it must hold: the bisectors split supplementary angles, differing by exactly $90^\circ$.
If one angle is $2\alpha$, the other is $2(90^\circ - \alpha)$ — half-lines $90^\circ$ apart.
So this perpendicularity is a structural fact, and a free sanity check every time.

segments.text: This Advanced example confirms the free check we keep mentioning — that the two bisectors are perpendicular.
Take the two bisectors we found in example one and verify their slopes multiply to minus one.
The first bisector, fourteen x minus one hundred twelve y plus one hundred one, has slope fourteen over one hundred twelve, which is one eighth.
The second, sixty four x plus eight y plus eighty one, has slope minus sixty four over eight, which is minus eight.
Their product is one eighth times minus eight, which is minus one — perpendicular, confirmed.
Now why it must always hold: the two bisectors split the two supplementary angles at the crossing, and those half-lines differ in direction by exactly ninety degrees.
If one full angle is two alpha, the other is two times ninety minus alpha, so their bisecting directions sit exactly ninety degrees apart.
So the perpendicularity is not a coincidence, it is structural — which makes it a free sanity check on every bisector computation you ever do.
यह Advanced example उस free check की पुष्टि करता है जो हम बार-बार कहते हैं — कि दो bisectors perpendicular हैं।
Example one में मिले दो bisectors लो और verify करो कि उनकी slopes multiply होकर minus one देती हैं।
पहला bisector, fourteen x minus one hundred twelve y plus one hundred one, की slope है fourteen over one hundred twelve, यानी one eighth।
दूसरा, sixty four x plus eight y plus eighty one, की slope है minus sixty four over eight, यानी minus eight।
इनका product है one eighth times minus eight, जो है minus one — perpendicular, confirmed।
अब यह हमेशा क्यों hold करता है: दो bisectors crossing पर दो supplementary angles को बाँटते हैं, और वे half-lines direction में ठीक ninety degrees का फ़र्क़ रखती हैं।
अगर एक full angle two alpha हो, तो दूसरा two times ninety minus alpha है, तो उनकी bisecting directions ठीक ninety degrees अलग बैठती हैं।
तो perpendicularity coincidence नहीं, structural है — जो इसे हर bisector computation पर एक free sanity check बना देती है।

board_events.text: Pitfalls: Angle Bisectors
Skipping the positive-constant normalization inverts every identification rule.
Acute/obtuse rule: with $c_1, c_2 > 0$, $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 > 0 \Rightarrow$ '+' obtuse; $< 0 \Rightarrow$ '+' acute.
Your two bisectors must satisfy $m_1 m_2 = -1$; if not, there is an arithmetic error.
Each line gets its own $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ — do not share one denominator.
Pro-tip: the origin's bisector is the '+' one after making constants positive — memorise that anchor.
Compute $a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2$ only when the question actually asks acute versus obtuse.
Don't compute everything — compute exactly what's asked.

segments.text: Let's close bisectors with the traps and one clean anchor to memorise.
Trap one, the biggest: skipping the positive-constant normalization. Every identification rule — origin, acute, obtuse — assumes both constants are positive, so normalize first, every single time.

Trap two: get the acute-obtuse direction right. With positive constants, a one a two plus b one b two positive means the plus bisector is obtuse; negative means it is acute. Write it down before deciding.
Trap three: your two bisectors must satisfy slope one times slope two equals minus one. If they do not, you have an arithmetic error somewhere — go back.
Trap four: each line gets its own root of a squared plus b squared. Do not share a single denominator across the two lines.
<whisper>And the one anchor to memorise: after making both constants positive, the origin's bisector is simply the plus one.</whisper>
Only reach for a one a two plus b one b two when the question specifically asks acute versus obtuse.
In short, do not compute everything — compute exactly what is asked, and no more.
Bisectors को traps और एक clean anchor के साथ बंद करते हैं।
Trap one, सबसे बड़ा: positive-constant normalization छोड़ना। हर identification rule — origin, acute, obtuse — मानता है कि दोनों constants positive हैं, तो पहले normalize करो, हर बार।
Trap two: acute-obtuse direction सही रखो। Positive constants के साथ, a one a two plus b one b two positive मतलब plus bisector obtuse; negative मतलब acute। decide करने से पहले लिख लो।
Trap three: तुम्हारे दो bisectors को slope one times slope two बराबर minus one satisfy करना चाहिए। अगर नहीं, तो कहीं arithmetic error है — वापस जाओ।
Trap four: हर line अपना root of a squared plus b squared रखती है। दोनों lines पर एक ही denominator share मत करो।
<whisper>और memorise करने का एक anchor: दोनों constants positive करने के बाद, origin का bisector बस plus वाला है।</whisper>
a one a two plus b one b two तभी उठाओ जब सवाल specifically acute बनाम obtuse माँगे।
संक्षेप में, सब कुछ मत compute करो — बस वही करो जो पूछा गया है, उससे ज़्यादा नहीं।
